p.src: Now when the generals heard that Kongming would not pursue the Wei army, they all entered his tent and said, “The Wei troops could not remain encamped because of the relentless rain, and so they have withdrawn. This is the perfect moment to pursue them. Why does the Prime Minister hold back?” Kongming replied, “Sima Yi is highly skilled in warfare. If he is retreating now, he is certain to have laid an ambush. If I pursue him, I shall fall straight into his trap. Better to let him go far away while I divide our forces, march directly out through Xie Valley, and seize Mount Qi, taking the men of Wei unawares.” The generals said, “There are other routes by which Chang’an may be taken. Why does the Prime Minister seek only Mount Qi?” Kongming replied, “Mount Qi is the gateway to Chang’an. Should troops come from any of the Longxi commanderies, they must pass through this place. Moreover, it faces the banks of the Wei River in front and rests against Xie Valley behind; troops may move out on the left or enter on the right, and ambushes may be laid there. It is ground made for warfare. That is why I mean to take it first and secure the advantage of the terrain.” All the generals bowed in admiration. Kongming ordered Wei Yan, Zhang Ni, Du Qiong, and Chen Shi to advance through Ji Valley; and Ma Dai, Wang Ping, Zhang Yi, and Ma Zhong to advance through Xie Valley; all were to rendezvous at Mount Qi. Once the dispositions were settled, Kongming personally led the main army, appointing Guan Xing and Liao Hua as the vanguard, and set out behind them.

p.src: Meanwhile, Cao Zhen and Sima Yi supervised the army from the rear. They sent a detachment to reconnoitre the old road to Chencang, and it returned with word that the Shu troops had not come. After another ten days’ march, all the troops left in ambush behind them returned, reporting that there was still no news whatever of the Shu army. Cao Zhen said, “The unbroken autumn rains have destroyed the plank roads. Can the men of Shu even know that we have withdrawn?” Sima Yi said, “The Shu army will emerge behind us.” Cao Zhen asked, “How do you know?” Sima Yi replied, “The weather has been clear for several days, yet the Shu troops have not pursued us. They have judged that I laid an ambush, and therefore let our army go far on; once all our troops have passed, they will seize Mount Qi.” Cao Zhen did not believe him. Sima Yi said, “Zidan, why will you not believe me? I am certain Kongming will come through the two valleys. You and I shall each guard the mouth of one valley, and set a limit of ten days. If no Shu troops come, I shall paint my face with rouge, dress in women’s clothes, and come to your camp to confess my fault.” Cao Zhen said, “If the Shu troops do come, I shall give you a jade belt bestowed by the Emperor and one of the imperial horses.” They immediately divided the army into two columns: Cao Zhen led his troops to encamp west of Mount Qi, at the mouth of Xie Valley; Sima Yi led his army to encamp east of Mount Qi, at the mouth of Ji Valley.

p.src: When both camps had been established, Sima Yi first led a detachment into ambush among the mountain valleys; the rest of the troops pitched camp along the strategic roads. Sima Yi changed his clothes, mingled among the common soldiers, and inspected every camp. On reaching one camp, he suddenly heard a junior commander look up to heaven and complain: “We were drenched by the rain for so long, yet they would not let us go back. Now they halt us here again and insist on settling a wager. How the soldiers suffer for it!” Hearing this, Sima Yi returned to his own camp, took his seat in the command tent, summoned all the generals before him, and singled out the offender. Sima Yi rebuked him: “The court maintains an army for a thousand days to employ it at the crucial hour. How dare you voice complaints and weaken the army’s morale!” The man denied the charge. Sima Yi called out his companions to testify, and the commander could no longer deny it. Sima Yi said, “This is no wager of mine; I mean to defeat the Shu army, so that every one of you may return to court with merit. Yet you uttered reckless complaints and brought punishment upon yourself!” He shouted for the guards to take the man out and behead him. Presently, the severed head was offered beneath the command tent. The generals were appalled. Sima Yi said, “All of you must devote yourselves fully to guarding against the Shu army. When you hear the signal cannon from my central command, advance from every side.” The generals received their orders and withdrew.

p.src: Meanwhile, the four generals Wei Yan, Zhang Ni, Chen Shi, and Du Qiong led twenty thousand troops forward through Ji Valley. While they were on the march, a sudden report came that the adviser Deng Zhi had arrived, and the four generals asked the reason for his coming. Deng Zhi said, “The Prime Minister has issued an order: if you emerge from Ji Valley, guard against an ambush by the Wei army and do not advance rashly.” Chen Shi said, “Why is the Prime Minister so full of doubts when employing troops? I judge that the Wei troops, battered by repeated downpours and with their clothes and armour ruined, must be hurrying home; how could they possibly have laid another ambush? If our forces advance at double speed now, we can win a great victory. Why has he ordered us to halt again?” Deng Zhi said, “Not one of the Prime Minister’s calculations misses, and not one of his plans fails. How dare you disobey his order?” Chen Shi laughed and said, “If the Prime Minister were truly so resourceful, the defeat at Jieting would never have occurred!” Wei Yan, recalling how Kongming had once refused to heed his plan, also laughed and said, “Had the Prime Minister listened to me and marched directly through Ziwu Valley, by now we would have taken not only Chang’an but Luoyang as well! What advantage is there in his stubborn insistence on advancing by Mount Qi? First he orders us to advance, and now he orders us to halt. How unclear his commands are!” Chen Shi said, “I have five thousand troops of my own. I shall march straight out of Ji Valley, reach Mount Qi first, and pitch camp there; then we shall see whether the Prime Minister is ashamed!” Deng Zhi tried repeatedly to stop him, but Chen Shi would not listen and led his five thousand troops straight out of Ji Valley. Deng Zhi had no choice but to hurry back and report to Kongming.

p.src: Chen Shi had led his troops only a few li when a cannon suddenly sounded and ambushing forces appeared on every side. When Chen Shi tried to retreat, Wei troops filled the mouth of the valley and enclosed him as tightly as an iron barrel. He charged left and right but could not break free. Suddenly, amid thunderous battle cries, a fierce detachment charged in. It was Wei Yan; he rescued Chen Shi and returned to the valley, but of the five thousand troops only four or five hundred wounded men and horses remained. The Wei troops pursued them from behind, but Du Qiong and Zhang Ni led troops to their aid, and only then did the Wei army withdraw. Only then did Chen Shi and Wei Yan believe that Kongming’s foresight was almost divine, but their regret came too late.

p.src: Meanwhile, Deng Zhi returned to Kongming and told him how insolently Wei Yan and Chen Shi had behaved. Kongming smiled and said, “Wei Yan has always borne the look of a rebel. I know that he constantly harbours resentment; I employ him only because I value his courage. In time, he is certain to cause trouble.” While he was speaking, a courier on a fleet horse suddenly arrived, reporting that Chen Shi had lost more than four thousand men and that only four or five hundred wounded troops and horses remained encamped in the valley. Kongming ordered Deng Zhi to return to Ji Valley and console Chen Shi, lest he cause a disturbance; at the same time, he summoned Ma Dai and Wang Ping and instructed them: “If Wei troops are guarding Xie Valley, lead your own units across the mountain ridges, march by night and lie hidden by day, and hasten to the left of Mount Qi, where you shall light fires as a signal.” He then summoned Ma Zhong and Zhang Yi and instructed them: “You too shall follow secluded mountain paths, hiding by day and marching at night, and proceed directly to the right of Mount Qi, where you shall light fires as a signal. Join Ma Dai and Wang Ping, and together raid Cao Zhen’s camp. I shall attack from within the valley on three sides, and the Wei army can then be defeated.” The four men received their orders and led their troops away by separate routes. Kongming then summoned Guan Xing and Liao Hua and gave them detailed secret instructions. The two men received the secret plan and led their troops away. Kongming himself led an elite force onward at double speed. While on the march, he also summoned Wu Ban and Wu Yi, entrusted them with a secret plan, and sent them ahead with troops.

p.src: Now Cao Zhen did not believe that the Shu troops would come; consequently, he grew careless and allowed his soldiers to rest. He merely waited for ten uneventful days to pass, intending then to shame Sima Yi. Seven days passed without incident, when suddenly someone reported that a small band of Shu soldiers had emerged from the valley. Cao Zhen ordered his deputy Qin Liang to lead five thousand troops on reconnaissance and under no circumstances allow the Shu forces to approach the border. Qin Liang accepted the order and had only just led his troops into the valley when his scouts saw the Shu soldiers withdraw. Qin Liang hurriedly led his troops in pursuit. After traveling fifty or sixty li without sighting the Shu soldiers, he grew suspicious and ordered his men to dismount and rest. Suddenly a mounted scout reported, “Shu troops lie in ambush ahead.” Qin Liang mounted and looked. Seeing great clouds of dust rising among the hills, he hastily ordered his soldiers to prepare for attack. Before long, tremendous battle cries erupted on every side: Wu Ban and Wu Yi charged from the front, while Guan Xing and Liao Hua led troops against their rear. Mountains hemmed them in on both sides, leaving no road of escape. The Shu troops on the hills shouted, “Those who dismount and surrender will be spared!” Most of the Wei troops surrendered. Qin Liang fought desperately, but Liao Hua struck him from his horse with a single slash and killed him.

p.src: Kongming detained the surrendered soldiers with the rear army, then gave their Wei uniforms and armor to five thousand Shu soldiers. Disguised as Wei troops and led by the four generals Guan Xing, Liao Hua, Wu Ban, and Wu Yi, they hastened straight toward Cao Zhen’s camp. First he sent a mounted messenger into the camp to say, “There were only a few Shu soldiers, and we have driven them all away.” Cao Zhen was delighted. Just then, it was reported that Commander Sima had sent a trusted man. Cao Zhen summoned the man and questioned him. The man said, “The Shu forces have now used an ambush to kill more than four thousand Wei soldiers. Commander Sima sends his regards and urges you to put the wager from your mind and devote yourself to careful defense.” Cao Zhen said, “There is not a single Shu soldier here.” He then dismissed the messenger and sent him back. Suddenly another report came: Qin Liang was returning with his troops. Cao Zhen himself came out of his tent to welcome him. By the time he reached the camp entrance, men reported that fires had broken out in both the front and rear. Cao Zhen hurried back to look behind the camp. There he saw Guan Xing, Liao Hua, Wu Ban, and Wu Yi directing the Shu forces as they stormed in through the front of the camp. Ma Dai and Wang Ping attacked from the rear. Ma Zhong and Zhang Yi likewise arrived at the head of their troops. Caught wholly unprepared, the Wei soldiers fled for their lives in every direction. The generals guarded Cao Zhen as he fled eastward, with the Shu troops pursuing from behind.

p.src: As Cao Zhen fled, thunderous battle cries suddenly arose and a body of troops charged toward him. Cao Zhen trembled with fear. But when he looked, he saw that it was Sima Yi. Sima Yi fought a fierce engagement, and only then did the Shu troops withdraw. Cao Zhen escaped, but was so ashamed that he wished the earth would swallow him. Sima Yi said, “Zhuge Liang has seized the advantageous ground at Mount Qi; we cannot remain here for long. We should encamp on the banks of the Wei River and devise a sound plan anew.” Cao Zhen asked, “Zhongda, how did you know that I had suffered this crushing defeat?” Sima Yi replied, “When the returning messenger reported that Zidan said there was not a single Shu soldier there, I judged that Kongming would secretly come to raid your camp. Thus I knew what would happen and came to your aid. And now, indeed, you have fallen into his trap. Let us say no more of the wager, but unite our hearts in serving the state.” Cao Zhen was deeply distressed. His pent-up anger turned to illness, and he took to his bed, unable to rise. The army encamped by the Wei River. Fearing disorder in the ranks, Sima Yi dared not allow Cao Zhen to command troops.

p.src: Meanwhile, Kongming drove his entire host forward and once more emerged at Mount Qi. After he had rewarded the troops, the four generals Wei Yan, Chen Shi, Du Qiong, and Zhang Ni entered his tent, bowed low, and begged punishment. Kongming asked, “Who was responsible for the army’s defeat?” Wei Yan said, “Chen Shi disobeyed orders and secretly entered the mouth of the valley, thereby bringing about our great defeat.” Chen Shi said, “Wei Yan told me to do it.” Kongming said, “He actually rescued you, yet you accuse him in return! You have already violated military orders; clever excuses are useless!” He immediately ordered the guards to take Chen Shi outside and behead him. A short while later, Chen Shi’s head was hung before the tent as a warning to the generals. At this time Kongming did not execute Wei Yan because he wished to preserve him for future use. p.src: Kongming told his generals, “Cao Zhen must be dead.” He wrote a reply agreeing to meet in battle the next day. The messenger departed. That night, Kongming entrusted Jiang Wei with a secret plan and instructed him how to carry it out. He also summoned Guan Xing and gave him detailed instructions. The next day, Kongming mobilized all the troops at Mount Qi and advanced to the banks of the Wei River. With the river on one side and mountains on the other, a broad, level plain stretched between them—a splendid battlefield indeed! The two armies faced each other, with archers holding the flanks of their formations in check. After three rolls of the drums, the central standards in the Wei formation parted. Sima Yi rode out, followed by his generals. They saw Kongming seated upright in his four-wheeled carriage, gently waving his feather fan. Sima Yi said, “Our sovereign followed the example of Yao’s abdication to Shun: the throne has passed between two emperors, who have ruled the Central Plain. That your two states of Shu and Wu have been allowed to exist is due solely to our sovereign’s generous benevolence and his fear of bringing harm upon the common people. You are but a plowman from Nanyang, ignorant of Heaven’s decree, yet you insist on invading us. By all reason, you deserve annihilation! If you reflect upon your errors and reform, you should return at once, each state guarding its own borders so that the balance of three powers may be maintained. Thus the people will be spared terrible suffering, and all of you may preserve your lives!” Kongming laughed and said, “The Former Emperor entrusted his orphaned heir to my care. How could I refuse to devote my heart and exhaust my strength in the campaign against the traitors? Your house of Cao will before long be destroyed by the Han. Your grandfather and father were both ministers of Han, and your family has lived for generations on Han stipends. Yet instead of seeking to repay that favor, you aid usurpers and rebels. Are you not ashamed?” Sima Yi’s face flushed with shame. “I shall settle with you once and for all which of us is the stronger! If you can defeat me, I swear never again to serve as a great general! But if you are defeated, return swiftly to your native home, and I shall do you no harm!”

He wrote a reply agreeing to meet in battle the next day.
The messenger departed.
That night, Kongming entrusted Jiang Wei with a secret plan and instructed him how to carry it out.
He also summoned Guan Xing and gave him detailed instructions.

The next day, Kongming mobilized all the troops at Mount Qi and advanced to the banks of the Wei River. With the river on one side and mountains on the other, a broad, level plain stretched between them—a splendid battlefield indeed!
The two armies faced each other, with archers holding the flanks of their formations in check.
After three rolls of the drums, the central standards in the Wei formation parted. Sima Yi rode out, followed by his generals.

p.src: Kongming asked, “Do you wish to pit general against general? Army against army? Or formation against formation?” Sima Yi replied, “Let us first compete in formations.” Kongming said, “Form your array first and let me see it.” Sima Yi returned beneath the central army’s command tent and waved a yellow flag in his hand. The troops to left and right moved and formed an array. He then mounted again, rode before the lines, and asked, “Do you recognize my formation?” Kongming laughed. “Even the lowliest general in my army could form it! This is the Primordial Unity Formation.” Sima Yi said, “Now form your array and let me see it.” Kongming entered his lines and gave a wave of his feather fan. He then returned to the front and asked, “Do you recognize my formation?” Sima Yi replied, “It is merely the Eight Trigrams Formation. How could I fail to recognize it?” Kongming said, “You may recognize it, but do you dare attack it?” Sima Yi replied, “Since I recognize it, why would I not dare attack?” Kongming said, “Then come and attack as you please.”

p.src: Sima Yi returned to his own lines and summoned the three generals Dai Ling, Zhang Hu, and Yue Lin. He instructed them: “The formation Kongming has deployed is arranged according to the eight gates: Rest, Life, Injury, Obstruction, Prospect, Death, Alarm, and Opening. You three are to break in through the Gate of Life due east, fight your way out through the Gate of Rest to the southwest, and then attack again through the Gate of Opening due north. Thus can this formation be broken. Take the utmost care!” Thereupon Dai Ling took the center, Zhang Hu the lead, and Yue Lin the rear; each commanding thirty horsemen, they charged in through the Gate of Life. Both armies raised battle cries in support. The three men fought their way into the Shu formation, only to find its ranks linked like a chain of walls, with no way to break through. In alarm, the three wheeled their horsemen around the edge of the formation and charged southwest, but the Shu troops stopped them with arrows, and again they could not break through. Within the formation, gate upon gate stood one behind another; how could they tell east from west, or south from north? The three generals could no longer look out for one another and could only rush about blindly; all they saw were vast clouds of sorrow and dense, baleful mist. Wherever shouts arose, the Wei soldiers were seized one after another, bound, and taken to the central command.

p.src: Kongming sat within his tent. Before him, Zhang Hu, Dai Ling, Yue Lin, and all ninety soldiers stood bound. Kongming laughed and said, “Even though I have captured you, there is nothing remarkable in it! I shall release you to return to Sima Yi. Tell him to study the books of war again and review the strategies of battle anew; it will not be too late then to come and decide which of us is superior. Since your lives are spared, you must leave behind your weapons and warhorses.” He then had their armor and clothing stripped off, their faces smeared with ink, and sent them out of the formation on foot. When Sima Yi saw them, he was furious. Turning to his generals, he said, “After suffering such a defeat and having our fighting spirit crushed, with what face can we return to meet the ministers of the Central Plains?” He immediately ordered all three divisions to assault the formation with no regard for death. Sima Yi himself drew his sword, led more than a hundred valiant officers, and urged the troops forward into the attack. Just as the two armies met, drums and horns suddenly sounded together behind the formation and a tremendous roar arose. A body of troops came charging from the southwest: it was Guan Xing. Sima Yi detached his rear division to resist them, then again drove the rest of his army forward into the fray. Suddenly the Wei troops fell into utter disorder. It was Jiang Wei, who had quietly led another body of troops into the attack. Attacked by the Shu troops from three directions, Sima Yi was greatly alarmed and hastily ordered a retreat. The Shu forces closed in from every side, and Sima Yi led his entire army in a desperate breakout to the south. Six or seven men in every ten of the Wei army were killed or wounded. Sima Yi withdrew to the southern bank of the Wei River, made camp, and held fast without emerging.

p.src: Kongming gathered his victorious troops and returned to Mount Qi. At that time Li Yan of Yong'an sent Commandant Gou An to escort grain and rice to the army and deliver it there. Gou An was fond of wine and had dawdled on the road, arriving ten days late. Kongming said in great anger, “In my army, provisions are the foremost concern. A delay of even three days merits execution! You are now ten days late—what possible defense can you offer?” He shouted an order to drag him out and behead him. Chief Clerk Yang Yi said: “Gou An is one of Li Yan's men, and moreover most of our money and provisions come from Western Sichuan. If you kill this man, no one will dare transport provisions hereafter.” Kongming therefore ordered the guards to untie Gou An, had him beaten eighty strokes, and released him. Having been punished, Gou An harbored resentment. That very night he took five or six mounted attendants and went straight to the Wei camp to surrender. Sima Yi summoned him, and Gou An bowed before him and related all that had happened. Sima Yi said, “Even so, Kongming is full of schemes, and your words are difficult to trust. If you can perform a great service for me, I shall then petition the Emperor for approval and secure you a post as a senior general.” Gou An said, “Whatever the task, I shall exert myself at once.” Sima Yi said, “Return to Chengdu and spread rumors that Kongming resents his sovereign and intends before long to proclaim himself emperor. If you can induce your lord to issue an edict recalling Kongming, that will be your achievement.”

p.src: Gou An agreed and went straight back to Chengdu. There he met with the eunuchs and spread rumors that Kongming, relying on his great achievements, would sooner or later usurp the state. The eunuchs were greatly alarmed when they heard this. They immediately entered the inner palace, reported it to the Emperor, and related the whole affair in detail. The Latter Lord exclaimed in alarm, “If that is so, what are we to do?” The eunuchs replied, “You should summon him back to Chengdu and strip him of his military authority, so as to prevent rebellion.” The Latter Lord issued an edict ordering Kongming to withdraw his army and return to court. Jiang Wan stepped forward from the ranks and memorialized, “Since the Prime Minister took the field, he has repeatedly won great victories. Why is he being recalled?” The Latter Lord said, “I have a confidential matter that I must discuss with the Prime Minister in person.” He immediately dispatched an envoy bearing the edict, with orders to travel through the night and summon Kongming back.

p.src: The envoy went straight to the great camp at Mount Qi. Kongming received him and, after accepting the edict, looked up to heaven and sighed: “My sovereign is young; there must be a treacherous minister at his side! Just when I am about to accomplish a great work, why am I being recalled? If I do not return, I shall be deceiving my sovereign. Yet if I obey the command and withdraw, it will be difficult ever to gain such an opportunity again.” Jiang Wei asked, “If our great army withdraws and Sima Yi takes advantage of the moment to pursue and attack, what shall we do?” Kongming said, “In withdrawing the army, I shall divide it into five columns. Today we shall first evacuate this camp. If there are a thousand soldiers in a camp, dig two thousand cooking hearths. Today dig three thousand hearths, tomorrow four thousand; as the army withdraws each day, increase the number of hearths along the way.” Yang Yi said, “Long ago, when Sun Bin captured Pang Juan, he used the method of increasing his troops while reducing the number of hearths; now, as the Prime Minister withdraws his troops, why do you increase the hearths?” Kongming said, “Sima Yi is highly skilled in the use of troops. When he learns that I am withdrawing, he will certainly pursue me; but suspecting that I have laid an ambush, he will surely count the hearths in each abandoned camp. When he sees that their number increases daily, he will not know whether my troops have withdrawn or not; beset by doubt, he will not dare pursue. Thus I may withdraw at leisure, with no danger of losing men.” He then gave the order to withdraw.

p.src: Now Sima Yi, reckoning that Gou An's scheme had succeeded, waited only for the Shu army to retreat, when he would launch a concerted pursuit. While he was still deliberating, a sudden report came that the Shu camp was empty and all its men and horses had departed. Because Kongming was so full of schemes, Sima Yi dared not pursue rashly. He personally led more than a hundred horsemen to inspect the Shu camp, ordered his soldiers to count the hearths, and then returned to his own camp. The next day, he again sent soldiers forward to the next camp to check the number of hearths. They returned and reported, “This camp has still more hearths than the previous one.” Sima Yi said to his generals, “I knew Kongming was full of schemes. Now he has indeed reinforced his army and increased the hearths. If I pursue him, I shall certainly fall into his trap. Better that we withdraw for now and devise a sound plan later.” Accordingly he withdrew his army and did not pursue. Without losing a single man, Kongming made his way toward Chengdu. Later, local people from the mouth of the Sichuan passes came and informed Sima Yi that when Kongming withdrew, they had seen no reinforcements arrive—only an increase in hearths. Sima Yi raised his face to heaven and sighed deeply: “Kongming has followed Yu Xu's method and deceived me! In strategy I am no match for him!” He then led his great army back to Luoyang. Indeed:
